To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

accelerator mass spectrometric (AMS) detection of [14C]adriamycin (ADR) DNA adducts in breast cancer cells at clinically-relevant ADR concentrations is now possible, and this has revealed a rapid accumulation of ADR-DNA adducts in the first hour of treatment, which is a previously unrecognised mechanism of ADR action.
the first direct evidence for Adriamycin– DNA adducts at clinical concentrations has been obtained using AMS.
accelerator mass spectrometric detection of Adriamycin-DNA adducts has been achieved for the first time at clinically relevant Adriamicin concentrations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of Adriamycin-DNA adducts in cancer cells.
the application of AMS to the detection of DNA damage and repair.
the development of a new, highly sensitive method for the measurement of drug–DNA adduct formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of AMS has enabled the detection of Adriamycin-DNA adducts at the clinically relevant concentrations for the first time.
the detection of Adriamycin-DNA adducts at the sub-micromole level is a reality.

the use of AMS for the measurement of [14C] Adriamycin– DNA adducts has enabled over three order of magnitude increased sensitivity compared with existing techniques and has revealed the formation of DNA adducts at concentrations relevant to the clinical use of Adriamycin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AMS is the first technology to allow direct measurement of clinically-relevant Adriacyclin–DNA adduct formation.
AMS is a highly sensitive technique for detecting Adriamycin– DNA adducts in cells, which can be applied to human tissue samples.
we have developed a highly sensitive and reproducible method for the detection of Adriamycin DNA adducts.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the detection of Adriamycin-DNA adducts at low drug concentration is feasible using AMS, which opens up new opportunities for investigating the role of these lesions in Adriamycin’s anti-tumour activity.
AMS has enabled the detection of DNA adduct formation at clinically-relevant drug concentrations for the first time, and has revealed a previously undetectable time course.
the clinically relevant Adriamycindrug concentration (25 nM, or 0.1 μg/ml) is sufficient to produce a significant number of Adriamycin-DNA adducts.
